key_insight: SlipSense shows that combining tactile pressure images with high-speed inertial sensing can detect slip faster and more reliably across different hardware settings. The key breakthrough is a multimodal tactile pipeline designed to measure and improve both latency and generalization, two aspects often ignored in prior work.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of detecting object slip early enough for dexterous manipulation, while also ensuring the detector works robustly across different tactile platforms and setups.
method: Builds on TacV5, a compact tactile sensor with a 32 x 32 piezoresistive array at 240 Hz and a 3-axis MEMS accelerometer at 8 kHz.
Uses the pressure array to capture spatial contact distribution and the accelerometer to capture high-frequency friction/slip dynamics.
Fuses multimodal tactile signals into a slip-detection framework optimized for low-latency response and cross-platform generalization.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners in robotics, this work highlights how multimodal sensing can improve real-world reliability beyond single-sensor approaches. It is especially relevant for robotic grasping, prosthetics, and manipulation systems that need fast reactions and deployment across different devices.

paper_title: SlipSense: Multimodal Tactile Learning for Low-Latency and Generalized Slip Detection
paper_authors: Tong Jian, Aditya Thurvas Senthil Kumar, Xinyi Li, Ziling Chen, Tianyu Dai
